title: Children's questions
hookLine: answer children's questions honestly, including "I don't know"
tomorrow: Gurveer's tying his first full turban. why call cloth a crown?

cards: Bebe Jaswant's kitchen, Monday, after school. Chilies from her garden are drying on a tray by the window. Fateh is eating a paratha and drawing a dinosaur, and Simran is meant to be doing calculus.
Then, mouth full, he asks it. When did God make the world? Before the dinosaurs or after?
Simran opens her mouth. She knows something about the dinosaurs. She knows nothing at all about the other half of that question, and she can feel herself about to make something up.
Bebe, at the stove, doesn't turn around. She says three words.

teach.b: Bebe says: nobody knows that. Then she turns around, spoon in hand, and says Guru Nanak asked the same question, and didn't pretend either. It's in Japji, the morning prayer, pauri twenty-one, on ang 4.
In paraphrase: what was that time, that moment, that day, that season, when the world was made? The pandits didn't find it, or it would be written in their Puranas.
The qazis didn't find it, or it would be written in their books. The yogi doesn't know it.
Only the Creator who made the world knows. Look at what Guru Nanak does there. He names the learned people of both neighbors around him, and he doesn't mock them.
He just says honestly: they don't know, and neither does any of us. The answer to the hardest question in the room is, I don't know. Then Bebe does the second half, which matters just as much.

teach.h: THEN SAY WHAT YOU DO KNOW.
teach.b: She tells Fateh what she does know. That the Granth opens with one Creator. That the world was made by the Hukam, the Order.
And that the dinosaurs came long before people did, which his science book can tell him more about than she can. Fateh nods, satisfied, and goes back to his dinosaur.
An honest I don't know didn't scare him. It made the true parts easier to trust.

how: Sikh parents and grandparents answer children's questions about God from Gurbani where they can, and Japji's twenty-first pauri gives them words for saying honestly that some things only the Creator knows.

o: the questions a granthi answers after the hukam
the catechism questions children recite before amrit
a child's questions, answered honestly, even with I don't know

games.q: Bebe's two-part answer — tap the pairs.
p: when did God make the world?
the pandits and qazis didn't find it

s: a good parent should always have an answer about God ready
even Guru Nanak, in Japji, says only the Creator knows when the world was made.
in Japji, Guru Nanak mocks the pandits and qazis for not knowing
he names them and says honestly that they didn't find it, and that only the Creator knows.
Japji's twenty-first pauri asks when the world was made
the time, the moment, the day, the season: and says only the Creator knows.

games.q: Simran is about to make up an answer to Fateh's question. what does Bebe do?
o: tells him a story about the world being made, so he's not left hanging.
says nobody knows, then tells him what she does know.
tells him that's a question for when he's older.
games.why: Bebe says nobody knows that, as Guru Nanak does in Japji, then gives him the parts she's sure of. the honest half makes the rest easier to trust.

practice: Close your eyes and bring up one question you can't answer: about God, about your life, about someone you love. Don't try to solve it. Let it sit there honestly unanswered, and notice what you do know around its edges.

wordCard.voice: Children's questions. Answered honestly, with I don't know where it's true, and what you do know next to it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Jap, the name of Guru Nanak's morning prayer, often called Japji.

carryVoice: Your line: honest answers. For the dinner table: nobody knows that, but here's what I do know. Good night.
